summary: This Best Current Practice describes iterative resolver behavior that sends large volumes of unnecessary queries to root and top-level domain servers. It offers implementation advice to resolver developers, drawn from observation of abnormal traffic at root servers and the com and net servers. It was later updated by RFC 9520.

plainLanguage.summary: Some DNS helpers keep asking the biggest directory the same silly questions. This tells the people who build them how to stop wasting its time.

questions: why do resolvers send too many queries to root servers
what is a lame dns server
why do dns resolvers query the root servers too much
how long should a resolver avoid a lame server
subtitle: What the authors of RFC 4697 saw DNS resolvers doing wrong at the root and com/net servers, and how to stop it.

tldr.problem: Root and top-level domain name servers receive large volumes of repeated, useless queries (requeries), almost always caused by deficient resolver, stub resolver or application implementations meeting an operational anomaly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogs eleven observed misbehaviors, such as re-asking the parent for NS records, hammering lame servers, and retrying endlessly behind firewalls, and gives implementors a recommendation for each.
tldr.outcome: None of the advice changes the core DNS protocol, and the document is a Best Current Practice (BCP 123). It was later updated by RFC 9520.

facts.label: Load increase seen at com/net
facts.value: 50% when several dozen popular zones failed

today: RFC 4697 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 123) and has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 9520. Read the two together.

sections.title: Why Requeries Matter
sections.content:
RFC 4697 grew out of watching traffic at two root name servers and at the thirteen com/net top-level domain (TLD) name servers. A large share of that traffic was requeries: the same question (<QNAME, QTYPE, QCLASS>) asked again and again at an unexpectedly high rate, sometimes from a single address and sometimes from many addresses at once.

The authors found that the cause is almost always a deficient iterative resolver, stub resolver or application, combined with an operational anomaly. The deficiencies include well-intentioned recovery attempts gone awry, insufficient caching of failures, giving up early when several levels of indirection must be followed, and aggressive retries. The anomalies include lame delegations, unusual glue records, and anything that makes every authoritative server for a zone unreachable, such as DoS attacks, crashes, maintenance, routing failures or congestion.

The document stresses that none of its recommended changes touches the core DNS protocol specification. It is guidance for people who write iterative resolvers.

The memo is mostly about the iterative resolver, the part of a recursive (caching) name server that sends queries. The name server part receives them. It uses "address record" to mean both A and AAAA records.
sections.plainLanguage: Some DNS programs keep asking the same question over and over. The people who run the biggest phone books in the world noticed and wrote down how to make it stop.

sections.title: Re-asking the Parent for Delegation
sections.content:
The first misbehavior is an iterative resolver that, after finding that every name server of a zone is unreachable, unavailable or lame, immediately sends a query for the zone's NS RRSet to one of the parent zone's servers. The standard algorithm in RFC 1034 does not call for such queries. When several dozen popular zones became unreachable on one occasion, the query load on the com/net servers increased by 50%.

The authors argue the check is pointless. If the resolver has just received a referral from the parent, asking again moments later will almost certainly return the same list. If instead it has cached an NS RRSet from the zone's own servers, that data is more trustworthy than the parent's, as RFC 2181 explains, so the parent's answer would be less trustworthy than what is already cached.

The recommendation is firm: an iterative resolver MUST NOT send a query for the NS RRSet of a non-responsive zone to that zone's parent's name servers. A zone is non-responsive when every server in its NS RRSet is lame, returns a server failure (RCODE=2), or is dead or unreachable according to Section 7.2 of RFC 2308.

Not every query to a parent is bad. If a cache holds an NS record but has lost the address record for an in-zone server, the resolver must ask the parent for that address (the glue), but that query is not a QTYPE=NS query.
sections.plainLanguage: If your friend's whole family is out and nobody answers the door, calling the phone book again every minute will not help. The number has not changed.

sections.title: Lame Servers and Failed Lookups
sections.content:
A lame server is a name server that has been delegated a zone but is not authoritative for it. Such a misconfiguration can last much longer than a transient outage, so repeatedly querying a known lame server is not useful.

Iterative resolvers SHOULD cache lame servers. If they do, the cache must be keyed on the tuple <zone name, class, server IP address>, and the resolver MUST refrain from querying the server for a configurable interval. A minimum of thirty minutes is RECOMMENDED. The key matters: a server can be lame for example.com yet authoritative for sub.example.com, so lameness must not spread automatically to subzones.

There is one exception. Some servers are lame only for certain query types, as described in RFC 4074. If all of a zone's servers are marked lame, the resolver SHOULD temporarily ignore the lameness status and query one or more of them.

Related failure handling appears in two more cases. Resolvers SHOULD be able to handle arbitrary levels of indirection from out-of-zone name servers (for example a delegation whose servers are named under a zone that itself depends on other servers) and SHOULD use a level-of-effort counter to avoid loops. The simplest cure is to name at least some of a zone's servers inside the zone itself. Name servers that fetch glue, and resolvers behind firewalls that pass queries but drop replies, SHOULD support throttling logic to detect queries sent with no responses received.
sections.plainLanguage: If one friend always says "wrong house, I do not live here", write that down and skip them for a while. But if every friend says it, try again, because maybe they only said it about one question.

sections.title: Glue Fetching and Firewalls
sections.content:
A name server doing glue fetching tries to include an address record for every NS record in the authority section of a referral, issuing its own queries when needed. This is a problem for authoritative-only servers whose administrators put them behind a device that blocks incoming replies. All glue-fetching queries then go unanswered, and the observed implementations retried excessively: one com/net server received hundreds of queries per second from a single such source.

The same pattern appears with resolvers behind misconfigured firewalls that allow queries out but not replies in. The retransmissions are useless, can continue for days or even weeks, and sometimes trigger intrusion detection alarms at the sender, whose administrators then complain that the root and TLD servers are attacking them. The failure can stay hidden when stub resolvers also query another, working recursive server, and the RFC notes that one popular stub resolver has a very aggressive retransmission schedule.

The recommendations are that administrators SHOULD NOT place iterative resolvers behind a firewall that lets queries through but blocks the replies, and that implementations SHOULD throttle themselves when queries are sent but no responses arrive.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine shouting a question across a canyon and never hearing the answer because someone put earmuffs on you. A good shouter stops after a few tries instead of shouting for weeks.

sections.title: Zone Configuration Mistakes
sections.content:
Two zone-side mistakes cause extra load on parent servers. The first is a missing trailing dot in the RDATA of NS records. A zone file for example.com that lists ns1.example.com without the final dot is parsed as ns1.example.com.example.com. Because NS records from the zone's own authoritative servers outrank the parent's referral, resolvers end up trying to resolve nonexistent names, and the bogus address queries show up frequently at the com/net servers.

An authoritative server can detect this, because a missing dot always yields a name under the zone's apex. It SHOULD warn when an NS record names a server below the apex with no matching address record in the zone and no delegated subzone where one could exist.

The second mistake is a zero TTL on a zone's NS records. That prevents caching, so the resolver must query the parent's servers every time it resolves a name in the zone. The RFC calls a zero TTL on a frequently changing RRSet extreme but permissible, yet says it rarely makes sense for NS records, except in anticipation of an upcoming change. Authoritative servers SHOULD issue a warning when loading a zone with a zero TTL on its NS RRSet.
sections.plainLanguage: If you forget the last dot in an address, the mail goes to a street that does not exist. And if you tell everyone to forget your address immediately, they have to ask the town hall every single time.

sections.title: Updates, Odd Queries and Server Choice
sections.content:
The rest of Section 2 covers four further issues.

  • Dynamic update probing. A popular dynamic update agent finds the closest enclosing zone by sending UPDATE messages (RFC 2136) to progressively higher-level zones, reaching the root and TLD servers. Failures teach it nothing. Agents SHOULD instead walk up the tree with SOA or NS queries, which can be cached, and send an UPDATE only once the zone is found. They SHOULD NOT probe with UPDATE messages.
  • Names that look like IPv4 addresses. The root servers receive many A queries for names such as 192.0.2.1, answered with Name Error (RCODE=3). Each needs its own negative cache entry. The RFC suggests delegating the numeric TLDs to a separate set of servers, for instance the AS 112 project's black hole servers, following the usual root zone change procedures.
  • Misdirected recursive queries. Root servers get queries with the Recursion Desired bit set because users point stub resolvers at them. A stub resolver could send a test query and check for the RA bit, and any error reporting SHOULD be throttled.
  • Name server selection. Resolvers SHOULD treat all NS records equally, not rely on their order (the first-listed a.gtld-servers.net receives disproportionate traffic), use the whole RRSet, favor the best-performing server by response time, and periodically recheck all servers instead of locking onto one.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not knock on every door in town one by one. Ask who lives where first, write the answer down, and take turns asking different helpers instead of always bothering the first one on the list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The misbehavior described in the document exposes the root and TLD name servers to increased risk of both intentional and unintentional Denial of Service attacks. The authors believe that following their recommendations will reduce the unnecessary traffic that reaches those servers, and so reduce the opportunity for an attacker to exploit such queries.

The RFC adds no new protocol features. It also states that there are no new internationalization considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone stops asking silly questions, the busy office has less noise, and it is harder for a prankster to bury it in calls.

viz.caption: KEY RULES FOR LAME SERVER HANDLING (RFC 4697)

items.title: Cache the lame server
items.text: Key it by zone name, class and server IP address.

items.title: Wait before retrying
items.text: A minimum interval of thirty minutes is RECOMMENDED.

items.title: All lame is a special case
items.text: If every server for the zone is marked lame, query one or more anyway.

items.title: Do not spread to subzones
items.text: Lame for example.com does not mean lame for sub.example.com.
